title: Ki Tisa: the thirteen attributes (Exodus 34:6–7)
hook: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering", chanted on holy days

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses in the cleft of the rock. Your line was seen only from behind. Did a moment look different looking back? Today, what Moses heard as God passed by. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

On a festival morning, as the doors of the ark open and the Torah scroll is about to come out, some congregations stop and sing the same words three times over. On Yom Kippur the words return again and again, through the day, until the closing service. No rabbi composed them. They come from Exodus: the words Moses heard in the cleft of the rock, as God passed by. Moses asked to see. What he got was something to hear.
screen: `THE ARK OPENS.` → `THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES.` → `WHAT MOSES HEARD.`

segments.voice: Moses has carved two new tablets and climbed back up the mountain. God descends in the cloud, passes before him, and calls out. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." It goes on: keeping mercy to the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin. Jewish tradition counts these as the thirteen attributes of mercy. Commentators divide the phrases in slightly different ways, but the count of thirteen holds. Now, the story behind the custom. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah, imagines God here wrapped in a prayer shawl like a leader of the service, showing Moses an order of prayer, and saying: whenever Israel sins, let them say this before Me, and I will forgive. So after the golden calf, the people are given words to come back with. Notice something about how they're said in the synagogue. In the Torah, verse seven goes on to say God will by no means clear the guilty. The prayer stops mid-sentence, just before that line, so that it ends on the word for clearing, for cleansing. The Talmud, in Yoma, reads the verse's two halves together: God clears those who return, and does not clear those who don't. And there's one more step. Another Talmudic passage, in Shabbat, reads these qualities as a pattern for people: as God is gracious and merciful, so you be gracious and merciful. The attributes are something to call on, and something to copy.
screen: `THE LORD, THE LORD.` · `THIRTEEN ATTRIBUTES OF MERCY.` · `GOD SHOWS AN ORDER OF PRAYER.` · `AS GOD IS MERCIFUL, SO BE YOU.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL AND GRACIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one quality and practice it. Settle, and breathe. Let the list pass slowly through your mind: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, true, forgiving. Which one do you have least of lately? Pick it. Then think of one person who'll test it today: a child, a coworker, a driver, yourself. Picture meeting them with that quality, just once. If you pray, you can say the opening words as they're written. If not, just hold the word you chose. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tisa. The portion where Moses hears the thirteen attributes of mercy: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in goodness and truth.
Your line: merciful and gracious. Today, practice your one quality on the person most likely to test it. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The thirteen attributes are chanted when the ark is opened on festivals in some communities, throughout the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days, on fast days, and again and again on Yom Kippur.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of God's good qualities.
what it means: the words Moses heard after the golden calf, given to the people as the way back, and chanted on holy days.
what a scholar hears: Rosh Hashanah 17b pictures God wrapped like a prayer leader teaching this order; the liturgy cuts 34:7 at v'nakeh (Yoma 86a discusses the verse's two halves).

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fixes: Ki Tisa does not end with 34:6-7 (it runs to 34:35), so 'the portion that ends with' corrected; the Talmud (Yoma 86a) discusses the verse's two halves, not the liturgy's cut, so the claim that it discusses 'a deliberate choice by the rabbis' was replaced. Also: narrator no longer asserts the words were not written by people; 'many congregations' and 'ever since' softened.
Exodus 34:6 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording and punctuation.
Ark-opening recitation: three times on festivals in many (especially Ashkenazi) communities, not on Shabbat; confirm wording 'many congregations'.
Rosh Hashanah 17b (God wrapped like a shaliach tzibbur, 'let them perform this order'): confirm.
Shabbat 133b (Abba Shaul: be like Him; as He is gracious and merciful) and Yoma 86a (the tension between 'clearing' and 'not clearing'); confirm references.
Different counts of the thirteen (e.g., whether 'the LORD, the LORD' counts as two attributes): stated generally.
